public_rationale: The claim says AI has no return on investment. The period checked runs from January 2025 to the post date, 2 June 2026. Wharton's 2025 enterprise survey, published 28 October 2025, found that three in four leaders see positive returns on generative AI investments. It also found that 72% formally measure generative AI ROI. Bain's April 2026 survey of 951 companies, published 1 June 2026 and cited in the post, reports a meaningful group of companies realizing the savings they targeted. Those findings meet the contract's contradiction condition. Some evidence supports a narrower point. In the same Bain survey, nearly 40% of companies that measured outcomes saw cost reductions of 10% or less, though 37% had targeted 11% to 20%. PwC data reported by Fortune in February 2026 show 56% of companies saying they get nothing out of AI yet. These figures show that returns are often absent or below target for many firms. They do not show that AI has no return at all.
limitations: The positive and negative return figures come from self-reported executive surveys, not audited results.
The surveys do not always net reported savings or returns against full AI costs.
The Wharton survey covers generative AI. Bain mixes automation, machine learning, generative AI and agents. The claim's scope (LLMs or all AI) is not fixed.
The Bain excerpt does not give the size of the group of companies that realized their targeted savings.
No audited net ROI figures for generative AI deployments were found.
JPMorgan's statement of about $2 billion in benefit for $2 billion in expense (October 2025) covers AI broadly and indicates rough break-even, so it is used only as context.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI has no return on investment.

statement.excerpt: The reason nobody can show you the ROI from AI is that AI does not have a return on investment.

from_speaker: nobody can show you the ROI from AI
AI does not have a return on investment
our_interpretation: Plain reading: spending on AI (mainly LLMs and generative AI, given the context) does not yield measurable returns. Credible measured or reported positive returns would count against it. Widespread failure to realize returns would count in its favor.
He names no period for this ongoing state. I use January 2025 to the post date (2 June 2026), the span of the main enterprise ROI surveys before the post. It is not limited to one quarter.
Self-reported executive surveys count as evidence, but they are weaker than audited figures.
criteria.support_condition: Credible studies or disclosures show that firms deploying AI generally fail to get returns that exceed costs, and none can document positive returns.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible studies or company disclosures document positive returns from AI investments for a meaningful share of firms.

evidence.excerpt: Three out of four leaders see positive returns on Gen AI investments.
evidence.explanation: A large enterprise survey finds most leaders report positive returns on generative AI, and 72% formally measure ROI. This contradicts 'AI does not have a return on investment', though it is self-reported.

evidence.excerpt: A meaningful group of companies is breaking the pattern. They are realizing the savings they targeted, deploying agents with genuine confidence, and funding the next wave from returns that actually materialized.
evidence.explanation: The survey the post itself cites reports a group of firms whose AI savings actually materialized, which counts against a total absence of ROI.

evidence.excerpt: nearly 40% of those who measured outcomes landed in the 0% to 10% bucket instead (see Figure 1). The technology worked. The value didn't arrive.
evidence.explanation: Shows that returns widely fall short of what was targeted. This backs his point that ROI is hard to show, though savings below target are not the same as zero savings.

evidence.excerpt: According to PwC data, AI adoption and productivity gains have been modest, with 56% of companies reporting they are getting “nothing out of” AI yet.
evidence.locator: section What's really happening with the labor market?, paragraph 4
evidence.explanation: A majority of companies report no return yet. This supports the claim for most firms, but not for all.

evidence.excerpt: “We have shown that for $2 billion of expense, we have about $2 billion of benefit,” Dimon told the outlet.
evidence.explanation: JPMorgan's CEO describes AI benefits roughly equal to costs. This covers AI broadly, including older machine learning, and implies about break-even, so it is context only.
